# Results — Study 962 (Do It Yourself) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim: a sector ETF is
mostly a handful of mega-caps, so hold the top N names yourself, skip the expense ratio
and keep the difference. We build that basket for **XLK**, **XLE** and **XLF** at depths
N = 3 / 5 / 10, under two weighting schemes — the fund's **published cap weights as of
2026-06-30** (the deliberate look-ahead) and the fund's **January-2011 top-10 held equal
weight, fixed from the first day of the sample** (the contemporaneous control) — rebalance
monthly with a one-day execution lag, and charge 5 bps one-way × NAV on traded turnover
plus a one-way charge to build the basket. Daily total-return closes (`yfinance`,
`auto_adjust=True`), 48 tickers. Sample 2011-01-03 → 2026-06-30. As-of **2026-06-30**
(the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| XLK, XLE, XLF + 44 constituent names + BIL (cash) | 2011-01-03 → 2026-06-30 | 3,895 | Fingerprint `1f3a3deb14a7` |

**Labelled non-tape inputs.** (1) Both holdings lists are **hardcoded PROXIES** — Yahoo!
serves no point-in-time holdings history, so the top-10s are typed in from public fund
fact sheets. (2) The January-2011 energy list is **survivor-only**: Anadarko (`APC`) and
Marathon Oil (`MRO`), genuine 2011 constituents, have no retrievable tape, so the two dead
names are replaced by the next *surviving* names down the sheet — and more generally every
name in every 2011 list is by construction one with a tape today. That biases the control
basket in the do-it-yourself investor's *favour*. (3) `GOOGL` and `BRK-B` are **ticker
proxies** for the lines a 2011 investor actually held (Google was one `GOOG` line until
the April-2014 class split). (4) **No tax anywhere, and dividends reinvest frictionlessly
at the close on both legs** — an assumption that again runs in the DIY basket's favour,
since an ETF sheds appreciated stock in kind while a private investor rebalancing ten names
realises the gain. (5) The **0.08%/yr** Select Sector expense ratio is quoted for context
only; it is never added anywhere, because the fund's own total-return close already carries
it (along with any securities-lending revenue it earns back).

## The headline — the contemporaneous basket vs the hindsight one

Both rows are the top-10 basket, monthly, 5 bps, blended equal-weight across the three
sectors.

| Basket | Ann. gap (DIY − fund) | HAC *t* | Tracking error | 95% bootstrap CI | Worst 12m |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Contemporaneous** (Jan-2011 top-10, equal weight) | **−0.76%** | **−0.58** | **5.13%** | [−3.21%, +1.69%] | −12.3% |
| **Hindsight** (2026 published cap weights) | **+6.08%** | **+6.10** | 3.85% | [+4.07%, +8.11%] | −8.1% |

The raw distance between those two rows is **+6.84%/yr** — but it is *not* all look-ahead,
because those two baskets differ in **two** things at once: which names, and how they are
weighted. The decomposition below separates them, and the honest look-ahead number is the
**+5.81%/yr** name-vintage term.

### Decomposing the +6.84%: name vintage vs weighting scheme

The control that identifies it is **eq2026** — *today's* names at **equal** weight. With
the weighting scheme pinned, `eq2026 − eq2011` is pure hindsight about membership;
`cap2026 − eq2026` is the separate effect of cap-weighting.

| Blended top-10 basket | Ann. gap | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| eq2011 — 2011 names, equal weight (contemporaneous) | −0.76% | −0.58 |
| **eq2026** — 2026 names, equal weight (*control*) | **+5.06%** | **+5.13** |
| cap2026 — 2026 names, published cap weights | +6.08% | +6.10 |

| Term | Blended | XLK | XLE | XLF |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Name vintage** (eq2026 − eq2011) — *the look-ahead* | **+5.81%** | +8.10% | +5.86% | +3.39% |
| Weighting scheme (cap2026 − eq2026) — *not hindsight* | +1.02% | +5.67% | −2.21% | −0.29% |
| Raw difference (cap2026 − eq2011) | +6.84% | +13.77% | +3.65% | +3.10% |

Two things fall out. The look-ahead term is **positive in all three sectors** and is the
robust part of the result: knowing in 2011 which names would top the fund in 2026 is worth
about **+5.8%/yr**. The weighting term is **not** — it is +5.67 pp in technology (cap
weighting concentrates the basket into the one name that ran away) and *negative* in energy
and financials. Attributing the whole +6.84% to hindsight would have credited the
look-ahead with an XLK-specific cap-weighting artefact. Strip the look-ahead out and the
contemporaneous gap is **negative** and indistinguishable from zero either way.

| **XLE** | −0.30% | −0.12 | 9.75% | [−5.24%, +4.58%] | 0.969 | 1.19 | +0.25 / +0.32 | **−81.8% / −71.3%** | −25.7% |

Not one sector clears |*t*| = 2, and no excess-of-cash Sharpe advantage survives: −0.04,

## Tracking error is the price, and it dwarfs the fee

| Basket | Tracking error | Fee saved | TE ÷ fee |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Blended top-10 | 5.13%/yr | 0.08%/yr | **64×** |
| XLK top-10 | 9.13%/yr | 0.08%/yr | **114×** |
| XLE top-10 | 9.75%/yr | 0.08%/yr | **122×** |
| XLK top-3 | 10.68%/yr | 0.08%/yr | **134×** |

### The power arithmetic

Blended TE of 5.13%/yr over 15.4 years gives a standard error on the annualised gap of
**1.31%/yr** — **16× the 0.08% fee being hunted**. To resolve an 0.08% fee at |*t*| = 2
against this tracking error you would need **≈ 16,500 years** of tape. The honest
statement is not "the fee saving is absent"; it is that **no test of this shape can ever
see it**, because the replication noise is three orders of magnitude larger.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2019-01-01)

| Fund | 2011–2018 gap (*t*) | TE | 2019–2026 gap (*t*) | TE |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| XLK | −1.35% (−0.82) | 5.02% | −6.94% (−1.73) | 12.04% |
| XLE | −1.42% (−0.74) | 5.72% | +0.80% (+0.17) | 12.72% |
| XLF | −0.25% (−0.17) | 4.38% | +4.46% (+1.58) | 7.76% |

No sector holds its sign across the two halves, and the tracking error roughly **doubles**
in the recent era — the funds have grown more top-heavy, so a fixed 2011 basket has drifted
further from what it was meant to replace. Nothing here is stable enough to bank.

## Cost and rebalance sweeps (XLK, contemporaneous top-10)

| One-way cost | Ann. gap | HAC *t* | | Rebalance | Ann. gap | HAC *t* | TE | Turnover/yr |
|---|--:|--:|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | −3.92% | −1.85 | | Monthly | −3.94% | −1.86 | 9.13% | 0.52 |
| 5 bps | −3.94% | −1.86 | | Quarterly | −3.65% | −1.73 | 9.01% | 0.31 |
| 25 bps | −4.04% | −1.91 | | Annual | −3.66% | −1.75 | 8.94% | 0.14 |
| 50 bps | −4.17% | −1.97 | | **Never** | −3.79% | **−2.38** | 7.08% | 0.00 |

Costs are not what decides this: turnover is only ~0.5×/yr, so the gross and net gaps
differ by 2 bps at the house rate. Long-only throughout, so no borrow cost applies.

**The full contemporaneous grid.** Sweeping every combination — 3 funds × 3 depths ×
4 rebalance frequencies = **36 cells** — exactly **one** clears |*t*| = 2: the
never-rebalanced XLK top-10, at **−2.38**, i.e. *losing* to the fund it replaced. We do
not present that as a finding. Thirty-six correlated cells searched at a 5% size would be
expected to throw up **≈1.8** hits by chance under a true null, so one hit is if anything
*fewer* than noise predicts. The honest reading of the grid is the absence of any cell in
the do-it-yourself investor's favour, not the presence of one against.

*2026 is a half-year (to 2026-06-30). Double-digit annual gaps in **both** directions are
routine. That is the lived experience of replacing a fund with ten names: not a quiet
0.08% saving, but a coin-flip that regularly costs or gains twenty percentage points.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

The panel plants a **deliberately fat** 2.00%/yr fee against a deliberately thin omitted
tail (10% of the fund), because that is the only regime in which a test of this shape has
any power at all:

- **Planted fee:** recovered gap **+1.96%/yr** (sd 0.13%), mean HAC *t* **+12.52**, fires
  on **6/6** seeds, TE 0.69%.
- **Null (no fee):** recovered gap **−0.06%/yr** (sd 0.13%), mean HAC *t* −0.39, fires on
  **0/6** seeds.

The detector recovers 98% of a planted fee and stays silent on the null. It is unbiased —
the real-tape non-result is a property of the market, not the harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** On a **contemporaneous** name list the blended annualised gap is
  **−0.76%** with HAC *t* = **−0.58** and a bootstrap CI [−3.21%, +1.69%] straddling
  zero; no sector clears |*t*| = 2 and no sign survives the era cut. The only |*t*| ≥ 2
  results in the basket's favour come from the **hindsight** basket (7 of its 9 cells;
  the blend is +6.08%/yr, *t* = +6.10). Decomposed against an equal-weight 2026 control,
  **+5.81%/yr of that is the look-ahead** in the membership list (positive in all three
  sectors) and +1.02%/yr is the separate cap- versus equal-weighting effect (positive
  only in XLK, negative in the other two) — so the honest look-ahead premium is +5.81%,
  not the raw +6.84%. Either way you are being paid for knowing which names would win,
  not for skipping a fee. Survivorship is named on this axis twice: the hindsight list is
  by construction a survivor list, and the 2011 control is survivor-conditional
  throughout — in energy explicitly so, two acquired constituents having no tape (a bias
  in the DIY basket's favour, which still fails to produce an edge).
- **Tradability — Mirage.** The fee you set out to save is **0.08%/yr**; the tracking
  error you accept to save it is **5.13%/yr** blended and **9-11%/yr** per sector — 64× to
  134× the prize. You also inherit the concentration: a worst rolling 12-month shortfall
  of −12.3% blended and −25.7% in energy, and an energy drawdown 10.5 pp *deeper* than the
  fund's. The trade is a near-certain small saving swapped for a large, uncompensated,
  two-sided risk.
- **What it really is.** Not a fee arbitrage but an **active bet** — a concentrated,
  fixed-list sector portfolio wearing an indexing costume. Priced as such, it earns no
  premium: the excess-of-cash Sharpe advantage over the fund is −0.04 / −0.07 / +0.00.
